newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Chicago water district head faces bribe charges.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Chicago water district head faces bribe charges.

text.p: A former president of the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago has been indicted on racketeering conspiracy, extortion and other offenses in connection with an ongoing investigation into public corruption, the U.S. Attorney's office in Chicago said.

Thomas Fuller, 62, allegedly conspired with a now-deceased commissioner and third man to take bribes totalling $31,400 from a cooperating defendant and an undercover FBI agent, U.S. Attorney James Burns said in an announcement Tuesday.
"The Water Reclamation District, like any public body, exists to serve the interests of all citizens, not to line the pockets of its elected officials and their cronies," Burns said.

Fuller served on the debt-issuing commission from 1978 until his defeat last year after his name surfaced in connection with the Operation Silver Shovel probe. He had been elected president by his fellow commissioners in 1993.
The multi-count indictment also charges a Fuller associate, James Blassingame, with racketeering conspiracy and other offenses for serving as a "bagman" to the deceased commissioner.
While not identified in the indictment, Commissioner Joseph Gardner, who died last year, has been named in other court documents.

The indictment alleges three separate racketeering acts from June 1992 to August 1994 evidencing acts of mail fraud. bribery, attempt and conspiracy to commit extortion and conspiracy to commit bribery and official misconduct, Burns said.
In one instance, bribes were paid to Fuller, Blassingame and Gardner to influence the award of a subcontract for work at district plants in two Chicago suburbs, the indictment contends.

In another instance, the undercover agent agreed to make a $10,000 contribution to Gardner's campaign fund for placement of a sham minority-owned business on the district's approved contractors list, the indictment contends.
Blassingame accepted a $10,000 cash payment for the commissioner, but Gardner never reported it as a campaign contribution, the indictment contends.

In the third episode, Christopher agreed to pay Blassingame $35,000, Gardner $10,000 and Fuller $5,000 to help one of his companies obtain a permit to use district land for crushing concrete and asphalt, the indictment contends.

Fuller allegedly accepted $5,000 from Christopher and Blassingame $2,000 from the undercover agent, but the district eventually rejected the land-use permit after an employee learned that Christopher controlled the company.
